passage:
Monday. In the sprint review the dashboard broke. Jaya, the team lead, said, “That was my call to skip testing. I'm sorry. Let's fix it together.” Rehana, three months into the job, had never heard a boss say that.

Thursday. The client praised the launch. Jaya said, “That was Ketan's idea and Meera's late nights. I just signed the emails.” Ketan sat up straighter, and Meera looked at her notes and smiled.

The next Tuesday, before choosing a new tool, Jaya asked, “Rehana, you've used both. What do you think?” Rehana's heart thumped. She answered, and Jaya wrote it down.

That night Rehana noticed she had never once feared Jaya's mood, and trusted every instruction more for it.

qa.q: What did Jaya say when the dashboard broke?
qa.a: Jaya said, “That was my call to skip testing. I'm sorry. Let's fix it together.”

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when Jaya asked what Rehana thought about the tools?
qa.a: Rehana felt nervous but valued, since a leader asked someone three months into the job for a view and wrote the answer down.

qa.q: What choice did Jaya make when the client praised the launch?
qa.a: Jaya credited Ketan's idea and Meera's late nights instead of taking the credit.

qa.q: What might Jaya be feeling when saying sorry in front of the team?
qa.a: Jaya may feel exposed but secure enough to admit the error, trusting that honesty earns more respect than pretending.

grounding: A newcomer watches a leader who admits mistakes, gives credit and asks for views, and comes to trust the leader more.

passage:
Saurabh, since you've just got your first team, listen to this. I'm Rafiq. At twenty-four I was the junior in Devraj sir's office. In my second week he sent a wrong figure to head office, and the next morning he told the whole room, “I got it wrong, and I'm sorry. Rafiq caught it.” I hadn't caught it, exactly; I had only asked a question. He gave me the credit anyway.

Every week he asked each of us, “What am I missing?” He listened even to the peon. When the company changed hands, half the office followed Devraj sir to his new firm. Nobody followed the new manager, who sat behind a closed door and signed papers. I've thought about that ever since.

qa.q: What did Devraj sir say the morning after sending the wrong figure?
qa.a: Devraj sir said, “I got it wrong, and I'm sorry. Rafiq caught it.”

qa.q: Why might Rafiq have remembered that morning for so long?
qa.a: Rafiq had never seen a senior person admit a mistake and share credit, so it left a trust and respect that lasted.

qa.q: What did Devraj sir do each week that showed he wanted the team's views?
qa.a: Devraj sir asked each person, “What am I missing?” and listened even to the peon.

qa.q: How might the peon have felt when asked, “What am I missing?”
qa.a: The peon probably felt surprised and respected, unused to being asked for a view.

grounding: An elder recalls a leader who admitted mistakes, gave credit and asked for views, and whom people followed by trust rather than position.
